steps.title: Design MN array master
steps.instruction: Create a 20 × 20 conical microneedle (MN) array (base 200 µm, height 450 µm, 400 µm spacing) on a 10 × 10 mm square base using NX Student Edition, save as .stl, convert to .gwl, and print with a Photonic Professional GT+ using IP‑Q resin and a 10× lens per manufacturer instructions.

steps.title: Clean printed master
steps.instruction: Submerge the printed master in 50 mL SU‑8 developer for ~2 min, then in 50 mL 100 % IPA for ~2 min; inspect under a microscope for bubbles, cracks, or broken tips.

steps.title: Prepare PMMA substrate
steps.instruction: Draw a 10 × 10 mm square in AutoCAD, export as .dwg, laser‑cut from a 3 mm thick PMMA sheet with double‑sided adhesive, and adhere this substrate to the backside of the master.

steps.title: Cast PDMS master mold
steps.instruction: Place the master in a Petri dish, mix 40 g Sylgard 184 base with 4 g curing agent, stir 2 min, degas under vacuum (>15 in Hg) for 30 min, pour over the master, degas again 30 min, cure at 80 °C for 2 h, cool, cut PDMS from the dish, peel off the master, trim excess PDMS, and inspect the mold for defects.

substeps.instruction: Mix 40 g base + 4 g curing agent in a cup; stir 2 min.
Degas mixture under vacuum (>15 in Hg) for 30 min.
Pour degassed PDMS onto master in Petri dish; ensure full coverage.
Degas the filled dish again for 30 min (or until bubbles disappear).
Cure at 80 °C for 2 h in a convection oven.
Cool to room temperature, cut PDMS out, peel master, trim excess.
Inspect mold under microscope for bubbles, voids, or uncured PDMS.

steps.title: Soak mold in IPA
steps.instruction: Submerge the PDMS master mold in 70 % IPA for 30 min, then air‑dry at room temperature for at least 1 h.

steps.title: Fill mold with SU‑8
steps.instruction: Drop‑cast SU‑8 2025 into the dried mold to fill the cavities, place the mold in a 50 mL centrifuge tube with MN tips pointing down, centrifuge at 2,500 × g for 15 min, UV‑cure at 365 nm for 3 min, remove the replica, and inspect for missing or cracked tips.

substeps.instruction: Pour SU‑8 2025 into mold until cavities are completely filled.
Insert mold into a 50 mL centrifuge tube, tips down.
Expose to 365 nm UV light for 3 min to cure.
Remove cured MN replica from mold with gloved hands.
Inspect replica under microscope for defects.

steps.title: Parylene coat MN replica
steps.instruction: Load the MN replica into a parylene deposition system, introduce 1 g parylene‑C dimer, run the coating cycle per the manufacturer’s protocol, then inspect for a uniform coating.

steps.title: Store MN replica
steps.instruction: Place the parylene‑coated MN replica in a Petri dish with tips facing upward and store at ambient conditions.

steps.title: Fabricate skin patch
steps.instruction: Design a 42 mm diameter circular patch with a 2 × 2 array of 11 × 11 mm cutouts (2 mm spacing) in AutoCAD, laser‑cut from a 1.5 mm thick PMMA sheet with double‑sided microfluidic tape, smooth interior edges with a Dremel, spray with 70 % IPA and wipe clean, then laser‑cut medical‑grade adhesive tape to the same design to create the sticker.

substeps.instruction: Create patch design (42 mm circle, 2 × 2 cutouts, 2 mm spacing).
Export as .dwg and laser‑cut from 1.5 mm PMMA with tape attached.
Smooth cutout edges using a Dremel rotary tool.
Spray patch with 70 % IPA and wipe with a Kimwipe.
Laser‑cut medical‑grade pressure‑sensitive adhesive tape to match the patch design, producing the sticker.

steps.title: Rinse MN array
steps.instruction: Remove the MN array from its Petri dish, rinse with 70 % IPA, and air‑dry at room temperature.

steps.title: Clean forearm
steps.instruction: Wipe the volunteer’s anterior forearm with a fresh alcohol prep pad and allow it to dry.

steps.title: Apply sticker to forearm
steps.instruction: Adhere the skin‑patch sticker to the cleaned forearm, ensuring proper alignment of the cutouts.

steps.title: Insert MNs first site
steps.instruction: Load the MN array into the spring‑loaded applicator per the manufacturer’s instructions, align it over one insertion site, place the applicator on the sticker, and press the button to insert the MNs.

steps.title: Repeat MN insertions per site
steps.instruction: Reload the applicator with the same MN array and repeat the insertion two more times at the same site, for a total of three insertions per site.

steps.title: Insert MNs all sites
steps.instruction: Perform the three‑insertion sequence (steps above) at each of the remaining three insertion sites, completing a total of 12 MN insertions.

steps.title: Wait 3 minutes post‑insertion
steps.instruction: Immediately after the twelfth insertion, start a timer for 3 minutes.

steps.title: Attach patch and vacuum cup
steps.instruction: While the 3‑minute timer runs, remove the backing from the sticker and adhere the skin patch so cutouts align, then remove the patch backing and attach the 42 mm vacuum cup securely to the patch.

steps.title: Generate and hold vacuum
steps.instruction: When the 3‑minute timer ends, attach the hand pump to the vacuum cup and pull the handle back fully once to create vacuum, then remove the pump and maintain the vacuum for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Observe ISF droplets
steps.instruction: During the 20‑minute vacuum, droplets of interstitial fluid should appear on the skin within approximately 5–10 minutes.

steps.title: Release vacuum and detach cup
steps.instruction: After 20 minutes, pull the pressure‑release valve on the cup to release vacuum and detach the cup from the skin patch.

steps.title: Collect ISF with capillary
steps.instruction: Use a 70 µL capillary tube to aspirate the ISF droplets, then transfer the fluid into a 0.5 mL low‑bind microcentrifuge tube using the capillary plunger.

steps.title: Remove patch and clean site
steps.instruction: Slowly peel the skin patch from the forearm, use adhesive remover wipes to lift remaining adhesive, and wipe the sampling site with a fresh alcohol prep pad.

steps.title: Sediment ISF sample
steps.instruction: Incubate the collected ISF at room temperature for 1 hour to allow particulates to settle.

steps.title: Centrifuge ISF sample
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the sample at 6,700 × g for 10 minutes in a microcentrifuge.

steps.title: Transfer supernatant
steps.instruction: Using a micropipette, transfer the clear supernatant to a new low‑bind microcentrifuge tube.

steps.title: Snap‑freeze supernatant
steps.instruction: Immerse the tube containing supernatant in liquid nitrogen for 5 minutes.

steps.title: Store frozen sample
steps.instruction: Store the snap‑frozen supernatant at –80 °C until further analysis.

description: Validation of protocol This protocol has been used and validated in the following research article: Jiang et al. [19]. Microneedle-based sampling of dermal interstitial fluid using a vacuum-assisted skin patch. Cell Reports Physical Science. The experimental procedure for fabricating the MN array via centrifugation-assisted replica molding is presented in Video S1, which results in the creation of mechanically robust and sharp MNs ( Figure 3A ). The strength of the MN array was validated through mechanical testing, as reported by Jiang et al. [19]. Force-displacement curves were generated for MN array replicas with different MN designs and array sizes, including the optimized MN design (base diameter = 200 μm, height = 450 μm) and array size (20 × 20) used in this protocol. This MN array can withstand up to 50 N of compression force, which is 1.5-fold larger than the force required to penetrate human skin, without exhibiting any signs of deformation ([19], Figure S1D). The penetration performance of the MNs was evaluated by inserting the MN array into porcine skin and performing histological analysis on skin sections, which revealed the formation of conical micropores in the epidermis ([19], Figure 2C ). Optical micrographs of the MN array after 12 skin insertions revealed that the MNs exhibited no discernible deformation or damage ([19], Figure S3D), validating the ability of the MN array to repeatedly penetrate human skin and generate micropores without fracturing or breaking. The ISF extraction efficiency was validated by sampling dermal ISF from 28 human volunteers, as reported by Jiang et al., [19]. ISF extracted using this technique was clear to light yellowish in color and generally more viscous than sweat ( Figure 3B -D). The average volume of ISF collected from all 28 volunteers was 20.8 ± 19.4 μL (mean ± SD) ( Figure 3E ).
